René Descartes

René Descartes (1596–1650) is the watershed figure. In the Meditations 1, he established the mind as the one indubitable reality (cogito ergo sum) while casting the entire external world into doubt—including the possibility that a malicious demon fabricates all sensory experience, a thought experiment that maps directly onto the brain-in-a-vat scenarios of modern philosophy. His dualism of res cogitans (thinking substance) and res extensa (extended substance) created the mind–body problem that neuroscience has been trying to dissolve ever since. Yet Descartes was also a mechanist: in L’Homme 2 and the Dioptrics 3, he modeled the body as hydraulic machinery, tracing sensory signals along nerve tubes to the pineal gland, producing a genuine (if wrong) mechanistic theory of the reflex arc.

Thomas Hobbes

Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) proposed the first explicitly computational theory of mind: “By ratiocination, I mean computation” 4. Thought is nothing but the addition and subtraction of internal names. Sensation is motion propagated from external objects through the sense organs to the brain, producing phantasms (internal representations) whose sequential processing constitutes reasoning. Where Descartes preserved a non-physical mind, Hobbes was an uncompromising materialist—there is nothing to the mind beyond matter in motion, and cognition is mechanical reckoning.

Baruch Spinoza

Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) dissolved Cartesian dualism by proposing that mind and body are not two substances but two attributes of a single substance [Ethics]. Every physical event in the brain has a corresponding mental description, and vice versa, but neither causes the other—they are one process described under two aspects. His concept of conatus, the striving of every being to persist in its own existence, has been noted as a philosophical antecedent of the free energy principle’s formalization of adaptive self-maintenance.

John Locke

John Locke (1632–1704) countered rationalist innatism with a systematic empiricism 5. The mind begins as “white paper,” devoid of content; all ideas arise from sensation (external experience) or reflection (the mind’s observation of its own operations). Complex ideas are built from simple ideas through combination, comparison, and abstraction. Locke’s further distinction between primary qualities (intrinsic to objects: solidity, extension, motion) and secondary qualities (produced by the object’s powers acting on the perceiver: color, sound, taste) reinforced the implication that much of experience is constructed, not copied.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) argued against Locke that the mind possesses innate structure: “Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses—except the intellect itself” 6. His concept of petites perceptions—tiny, unconscious perceptions that individually fall below the threshold of awareness but collectively shape conscious experience (as the roar of the sea is composed of individually inaudible waves)—is a remarkable anticipation of subliminal processing and hierarchical sensory integration. The mill argument 7 anticipates the hard problem: if one could walk through a brain enlarged to the size of a mill, one would find only mechanical parts pushing against each other, and nowhere would one find perception.

Thomas Willis

Thomas Willis (1621–1675) effectively founded the discipline of neurology. In Cerebri Anatome 8, illustrated by Christopher Wren, he produced the most detailed neuroanatomy of his era, identifying and naming structures including the arterial circle that bears his name, the striate body, and the corpus striatum. More consequential than his anatomy was a theoretical revolution: Willis relocated mental functions from the ventricular fluid—where Galenic tradition had housed them for over a millennium—to the brain’s solid tissue, its cortical convolutions and subcortical nuclei. Imagination and memory, he argued, reside in the cerebral gyri; involuntary and instinctive motion is governed by the cerebellum. With Willis, the brain ceased to be a passive container of animal spirits and became an active, structurally differentiated organ whose regional architecture maps onto distinct cognitive operations.

Nicolas Malebranche

Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715) developed his theory of perception in De la recherche de la vérité 9, a work that is simultaneously a systematic epistemology and a remarkably thorough catalog of perceptual error, sensory illusion, and cognitive bias. The senses, he argued, are systematically unreliable guides to the nature of things; they were designed by God for the preservation of the body, not the discovery of truth, and must be corrected by reason at every turn. His occasionalism—the doctrine that God is the sole true cause of every event, with physical and mental occurrences serving merely as “occasions” for divine action—can be read, if one substitutes the generative model for God, as a striking early intuition that the proximate cause of perceptual experience lies not in the external stimulus but in the internal system that generates the percept.
